source_reviews.independent_solution: In the ordinary hot-cathode DC carbon-arc explanation, the negative electrode supplies emitted electrons. Strong cathode cooling reduces thermionic supply sharply; if it can no longer sustain the required discharge current, the arc weakens and may extinguish. The positive anode primarily collects the electrons, so cooling it is not the same direct interruption of cathode thermionic emission. This does not imply that anode cooling has no effect: electrode heat balance, gas/plasma conditions and circuit response are coupled. Without final temperatures and operating conditions the source does not fix an exact transient or guarantee identical behavior in every arc regime.

coverage.evidence: Both printed cooling interventions remain in one comparison unit. The visible hot-cathode model is explicitly authored, not inserted as source data. Recognition/writing and unspecified exact outcome/time losses are recorded in intent and coverage; no source value or measured cooling history is invented.

source_reviews.independent_solution: Combustion supplies charge carriers in the flame, including positive ions and negative carriers. The electric field acts on them; collisional momentum transfer to the neutral gas produces electrohydrodynamic motion. Positive ions are driven toward the negative electrode, while electrons and negative ions have the opposite electric-force direction. The stated cathode-directed bending is consistent with the net field-driven force/flow asymmetry in that observed configuration, not with every neutral gas molecule directly feeling the same electric force. The source does not supply the carrier distributions or flow field needed to derive a quantitative universal one-way wind. Flame bending and the detailed ionic-wind directions must not be equated, and the entire flame need not be declared a uniformly positively charged body.

mathematics.independent_solution: In the stated ordinary thermionic model, cooling the cathode reduces its emitted-electron supply; loss of sufficient uncompensated supply can extinguish the discharge. Cooling the anode is not the same direct change to cathode emission, but heat transfer, ablation and plasma/circuit balance can affect persistence. Temperature alone does not remove a supply-imposed field or increase thermionic emission. The complete set is A,B.

option_checks.evidence: The lowered thermionic supply and explicit insufficient-supply/no-compensation condition support possible extinction, while avoiding a guarantee for every temperature decrease.

Anode cooling does not directly suppress cathode thermal emission in the same way. Continuation is conditional on adequate emission, ionization and energy balance, not guaranteed for all cooling strengths.

For a fixed applied field and the same charge, the electric-force expression has no such greater-force-by-colder-surface dependence. Lower temperature reduces, rather than increases, the stated thermionic supply.
Cooling either rod does not necessarily remove the field of a still-connected power supply; an otherwise sustained discharge is a counterexample to guaranteed instantaneous extinction.

Electron collection is not the anode's only thermal interaction. Changes to heat transfer and carbon ablation can affect the arc column and stability, so universal immunity to arbitrarily strong anode cooling is unsupported and false.

mathematics.independent_solution: Positive ions experience electric force toward the negative electrode; electrons and negative ions have the opposite force direction. Their collisions transfer momentum to neutral gas. In the stated configuration the net electrohydrodynamic response can account for the flame deformation, without concluding that all local flow is cathode-directed. B reverses both force signs; C invents a uniform charge-independent thermal force; D erases negative carriers and asserts universal geometry-independent behavior. Only A is correct.

option_checks.evidence: The carrier-force directions and collisional transfer are correct, and the configuration-specific 'can' claim does not prescribe all local flow or a universal net carrier density.

Negative carriers are electrically forced toward the positive plate and positive ions toward the negative plate; the stated signs are reversed. This verdict concerns the claimed electric-force drift, not arbitrary total trajectories with convection.

High temperature by itself does not give neutral molecules a common electric force pointing at the negative plate. Possible polarization in other field configurations does not rescue this uniform heat-only directional claim.

An ordinary flame can contain negative carriers as well as positive ions, not just a uniformly positive body. Electric-field and flow/electrode conditions matter, contradicting the every-field/every-arrangement bending assertion.
